short: Rhythm is the pattern of when sounds happen.
It is made of the gaps between sounds as much as the sounds.

studyNotes.echo: Here the rhythm changes the moment the early tap arrives.

short: A beat is one single sound in a steady pattern.
Each beat here marks one site waking up.

studyNotes.meter: Here some beats go missing in a regular way.

short: Tempo is how fast the beats come.
A quicker tempo means shorter gaps between beats.

studyNotes.prelude: Here your tapping sets the tempo of the heart.

short: A rest is a beat that stays silent.
The pattern carries on, with one sound left out.

studyNotes.meter: Here a rest appears when one wave fails to get through.

short: A pause is a longer silence between two beats.
It gives the ear a moment before the next sound.

studyNotes.prelude: Here a pause follows the pacing, before the natural rhythm returns.

short: A melody is a line of notes heard one after another.
The order of the notes is what you recognise.

studyNotes.retrograde: Here the same line of notes comes round in both directions.

short: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time.
The notes follow each other in a steady order.

studyNotes.echo: Here the atrium and ventricle sound one after the other.

short: A chord is several notes sounding at once.
When notes fall very close together they blend into one.

studyNotes.echo: Here the atrium and ventricle sound almost together.

short: An echo is a sound that comes back a moment later.
It repeats something you have just heard.

studyNotes.echo: Here one extra beat returns to the atrium after the ventricle.

short: A round is a tune that one voice starts and others join later.
Every voice sings the same notes, a little apart.

studyNotes.canon: Here two waves chase each other around the same ring.

short: Faster means the beats come closer together.
The pattern stays the same but moves along more quickly.

studyNotes.prelude: Here the heart speeds up gradually as it recovers.

short: Slower means the beats spread further apart.
The pattern stays the same but takes more time.

studyNotes.ostinato: Here slower conduction lets the lower voice keep up.

short: Hemiola is three beats of one voice against two of another.
The two voices meet again after every full set.

studyNotes.hemiola: Here it appears when the two pacemakers lock three to two.

short: An ostinato is a short figure repeated again and again.
Other voices change while it keeps going underneath.

studyNotes.ostinato: Here the fast atrial circuit repeats while the lower voice answers.

short: Retrograde means playing a melody backwards, from its last note to its first.
The same notes are heard in reverse order.

studyNotes.retrograde: Here the second circuit visits the same sites in reverse.

short: A canon is one melody sung by voices that start at different times.
Each voice copies the first exactly.

studyNotes.canon: Here two waves circle the ring, half a lap apart.

short: Phasing is two steady patterns drifting slowly apart and back together.
Their small speed difference creates ever-changing overlaps.

studyNotes.hemiola: Here the two pacemakers drift until they begin to listen to each other.

short: Meter is how beats gather into regular groups, such as threes or fours.
The first beat of each group feels stronger.

studyNotes.meter: Here groups form as beats drop out at a regular interval.

short: A fermata is a held note or silence, lasting longer than written.
The player decides when the music moves on.

studyNotes.prelude: Here the long pause after pacing is held until the heart resumes.

short: Accelerando means gradually getting faster.
Each gap is a little shorter than the last.

studyNotes.prelude: Here the beats quicken step by step back to the resting pace.

short: Rubato means bending the timing a little, giving and taking time.
The beat sways but stays together overall.

studyNotes.prelude: Here the gentle sway of breathing stretches and shortens the gaps.

short: A suspension is a note held back a moment before it arrives.
The delay creates a small wish for the next sound.

studyNotes.echo: Here the ventricle arrives suddenly later than the atrium led you to expect.

short: Polyrhythm is two different beat patterns sounding together.
Each keeps its own count at the same time.

studyNotes.hemiola: Here the two voices keep different counts until they lock.
